citations.quote:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space and let $n\ge0$. Write
$\operatorname{End}(V)$ for the $\mathbb C$-vector space of all linear maps
$V\to V$, and $\operatorname{GL}(V)\subseteq\operatorname{End}(V)$ for the
invertible ones
([[def-finite-dimensional-representation-of-a-group-over-a-field]]).
All tensor products below are over $\mathbb C$.

**The tensor power.** For $n\ge1$ fix the parenthesization
$$E_n\;:=\;V^{\otimes n}\;:=\;\underbrace{V\otimes_{\mathbb C}\cdots\otimes_{\mathbb C}V}_{n\text{ factors}},\qquad V^{\otimes0}\;:=\;\mathbb C,$$
and write $v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n$ for the elementary tensor of
$(v_1,\dots,v_n)\in V^n$; for $n=0$ the unique elementary tensor is $1\in\mathbb C$.
By [[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]] the
assignment $(v_1,\dots,v_n)\mapsto v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n$ is
$\mathbb C$-multilinear and every element of $E_n$ is a finite
$\mathbb C$-linear combination of elementary tensors; for $n=0$ this means
$c=c\cdot1$ for $c\in\mathbb C$. If $e_1,\dots,e_d$ is a $\mathbb C$-basis of
$V$, then by iterating [[thm-tensor-product-basis-from-bases]] the $d^n$ tensors
$e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_n}$ form a $\mathbb C$-basis of $E_n$, so
$E_n$ is finite-dimensional.

**Place permutations: the left $S_n$-action.** Let $S_n$ be the symmetric
group of the set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]). For
$\sigma\in S_n$ define, on elementary tensors,
$$\sigma\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\;:=\;v_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\sigma^{-1}(n)}.$$
The right-hand side depends $\mathbb C$-multilinearly on
$(v_1,\dots,v_n)$, so by the universal property in
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]] there is a
unique $\mathbb C$-linear map $E_n\to E_n$ with this value on every elementary
tensor. Uniqueness is what makes the rule well defined on all of $E_n$, since
the elementary tensors span. The identity permutation acts trivially, and for
$\sigma,\tau\in S_n$ and every elementary tensor,
$$(\sigma\tau)\cdot\bigl(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n\bigr)=v_{(\sigma\tau)^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{(\sigma\tau)^{-1}(n)}=v_{\tau^{-1}(\sigma^{-1}(1))}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\tau^{-1}(\sigma^{-1}(n))},$$
while $\tau\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_{\tau^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\tau^{-1}(n)}$
and hence
$$\sigma\cdot\bigl(\tau\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\bigr)=v_{\tau^{-1}(\sigma^{-1}(1))}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\tau^{-1}(\sigma^{-1}(n))}.$$
The two agree, so the assignments constitute a left action of the group $S_n$
on $E_n$; equivalently $E_n$ is a left module over $S_n$
([[def-finite-dimensional-representation-of-a-group-over-a-field]]).
For $n=0$ the group $S_0$ is trivial and acts on $E_0=\mathbb C$ by the
identity.

**Diagonal linear action.** For $g\in\operatorname{GL}(V)$ define, on
elementary tensors,
$$g^{\otimes n}\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\;:=\;gv_1\otimes\cdots\otimes gv_n,$$
again first on elementary tensors by multilinearity and then uniquely on
$E_n$. Since $g$ and $h$ are linear, the two assignments compose in the
expected way: on elementary tensors,
$$(gh)^{\otimes n}\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=g(hv_1)\otimes\cdots\otimes g(hv_n)=g^{\otimes n}\cdot\bigl(h^{\otimes n}\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\bigr),$$
and $(\mathrm{id}_V)^{\otimes n}$ is the identity. In particular
$(g^{-1})^{\otimes n}$ is the inverse of $g^{\otimes n}$. For $n=0$ every
diagonal operator is the identity on $\mathbb C$.
Thus $g\mapsto g^{\otimes n}$ is a group homomorphism
$\operatorname{GL}(V)\to\operatorname{GL}(E_n)$, that is, a finite-dimensional
representation of the group $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ on $E_n$.

**The two actions commute.** For $\sigma\in S_n$, $g\in\operatorname{GL}(V)$
and an elementary tensor,
$$\sigma\cdot\bigl(g^{\otimes n}\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\bigr)=gv_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes gv_{\sigma^{-1}(n)}=g^{\otimes n}\cdot\bigl(\sigma\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\bigr),$$
so the two linear maps $\sigma\cdot(-)$ and $g^{\otimes n}\cdot(-)$ commute;
equivalently, every $g^{\otimes n}$ is an $S_n$-equivariant endomorphism of
$E_n$ ([[def-intertwiner-equivalent-and-faithful-representations]]).

**The diagonal infinitesimal operator.** For $T\in\operatorname{End}(V)$ put
$$\Delta(T)\;:=\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf 1^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes T\otimes\mathbf 1^{\otimes(n-i)}\ \in\ \operatorname{End}(E_n),$$
where $\mathbf 1=\mathrm{id}_V$ and the sum is $0$ for $n=0$. Each summand
lies in $\operatorname{End}(E_n)$, and $\Delta:\operatorname{End}(V)\to
\operatorname{End}(E_n)$ is $\mathbb C$-linear. It is the first coefficient of
the diagonal action along the line $t\mapsto\mathbf 1+tT$. In this polynomial
calculation, $(\mathbf 1+tT)^{\otimes n}$ is the tensor power of the
endomorphism $\mathbf 1+tT$; it agrees with the $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ action
whenever that endomorphism is invertible. For every $t\in\mathbb C$ one
computes, on elementary tensors,
$$(\mathbf 1+tT)^{\otimes n}\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}t^k\sum_{1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n}w_{i_1,\dots,i_k},\qquad (w_{i_1,\dots,i_k})_j=\begin{cases}Tv_j,&j\in\{i_1,\dots,i_k\},\\ v_j,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
the coefficient of $t$ being $\Delta(T)\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)$
(zero when $n=0$); both sides
are polynomials in $t$ with values in the finite-dimensional space $E_n$
described on a spanning set. Finally let
$$A_n\;:=\;\text{the unital }\mathbb C\text{-subalgebra of }\operatorname{End}(E_n)\text{ generated by }\{\Delta(T):T\in\operatorname{End}(V)\};$$
this is the image of the diagonal action of the universal enveloping algebra
$U(\mathfrak{gl}(V))$ on $E_n$, defined here as that generated algebra, with
no Lie-theoretic input.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. If $M$ is free with basis $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $N$ is free with basis $(f_j)_{j\in J}$, then $M\otimes_RN$ is free with basis

$$\bigl(e_i\otimes f_j\bigr)_{(i,j)\in I\times J}.$$

Equivalently, the canonical map $R^{(I\times J)}\to M\otimes_RN$ sending the standard basis vector at $(i,j)$ to $e_i\otimes f_j$ is an isomorphism. This includes an empty basis in either factor.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

A subset $B \subseteq V$ is a **basis of $V$** when

- **(B1)** $B$ is linearly independent ([[def-linear-independence]]), and
- **(B2)** $B$ spans $V$, that is $\operatorname{span}(B) = V$
  ([[def-linear-combination-and-span]], which is where the words *spans* and
  *spanning set* are fixed; they are not redefined here).

**The empty set is a basis of the zero space, and of nothing else.**
$\varnothing$ is linearly independent ([[def-linear-independence]]) and
$\operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
([[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]]), so $\varnothing$ is a basis of
$V$ exactly when $V = \{0_V\}$. This is the case $n = 0$ from which every
induction on this page starts, and it is a genuine case rather than a convention.

### Ordered bases

An **ordered basis of $V$** is a finite list $v : n \to V$, with $n \in
\mathbb{N}$ and $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ the von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), such that $v$ is
injective ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]) and its image $v[n]$ is a
basis of $V$.

By claim 6 of [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]], a list is linearly
independent exactly when it is injective with linearly independent image, so an
ordered basis is equally described as a **linearly independent list $v : n \to V$
with $\operatorname{span}(v[n]) = V$**: the injectivity does not have to be
imposed separately. The empty list is the ordered basis of the zero space.

An ordered basis is a list, so it carries an order; a basis is a set, so it does
not. Reordering an ordered basis gives a different ordered basis with the same
image, and the coordinates of
[[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]] are attached to the
list, not to the set.

### Bases of a linear subspace

Let $U$ be a linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]), which is itself a
vector space over $F$, with the addition, the zero vector and the scalar
multiplication of $V$ restricted to $U$. For $A \subseteq U$ the two readings of
"$A$ is a basis" — computed inside $U$, or computed inside $V$ — agree, so the
phrase needs no disambiguation below.

- **Independence agrees.** The finite sums $\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i a_i$ of a list
  $a : n \to U$ are given by the same recursion in $U$ as in $V$
  ([[def-monoid-finite-product]]), the base value $0_V$ and the operation $+$
  being literally those of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). So a list into $U$ has
  the same sums whichever space it is read in, and the vanishing condition of
  [[def-linear-independence]] is the same condition in both.
- **The span agrees.** A subset of $U$ is a linear subspace of $U$ exactly when it
  is a linear subspace of $V$, conditions (W1), (W2), (W3) being the same
  conditions in either reading. Now $\operatorname{span}_V(A) \subseteq U$, since
  $U$ is a linear subspace of $V$ containing $A$ and the span is contained in
  every such subspace; so $\operatorname{span}_V(A)$ is a linear subspace of $U$
  containing $A$, whence $\operatorname{span}_U(A) \subseteq \operatorname{span}_V(A)$.
  Conversely $\operatorname{span}_U(A)$ is a linear subspace of $V$ containing
  $A$, whence $\operatorname{span}_V(A) \subseteq \operatorname{span}_U(A)$. The
  two are therefore equal, and we write $\operatorname{span}(A)$ for both.

Consequently $A \subseteq U$ is a basis of the vector space $U$ if and only if
$A$ is linearly independent as a subset of $V$ and $\operatorname{span}(A) = U$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $M_1,\ldots,M_k$ be a finite list of $R$-modules. Any parenthesized tensor product

$$T=M_1\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RM_k$$

represents $R$-multilinear maps from $M_1\times\cdots\times M_k$: for every $R$-module $P$, composition with $(m_1,\ldots,m_k)\mapsto m_1\otimes\cdots\otimes m_k$ is a bijection from $\operatorname{Hom}_R(T,P)$ to the set of multilinear maps into $P$. Different parenthesizations are connected by the unique isomorphism preserving pure tensors.

For $k=0$, take $T=R$ and identify zero-variable multilinear maps with chosen elements of $P$. For $k=1$, take $T=M_1$.

For a field $F$ and naturals $m,n$,
$\dim_FM_{m\times n}(F)=mn$. Consequently, for finite-dimensional $F$-vector
spaces $V,W$,

$$\dim_F\mathcal L(V,W)=(\dim_FV)(\dim_FW).$$

Let $V,W$ be finite-dimensional vector spaces over $F$, with ordered bases
$\mathcal B=(b_j)_{j<n}$ and $\mathcal C=(c_i)_{i<m}$. The map

$$\Phi:\mathcal L(V,W)\to M_{m\times n}(F),\qquad \Phi(T)=[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C},$$

is a vector-space isomorphism.
Let $D$ be an integral domain. A nonzero polynomial $f\in D[x]$ of degree $n$ has at most $n$ distinct roots in $D$.

Let $T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$. Choose an ordered basis $\mathcal B$ and define

$$\chi_T(x):=\chi_{[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}}(x).$$

Matrices representing the same endomorphism in different ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial. Hence $\chi_T$ is independent of $\mathcal B$. When $V=\{0_V\}$, the empty ordered basis gives $\chi_T=1$.

Let $T:V\to V$ be a linear operator on a finite-dimensional vector space over
a field $F$. Then $T$ is invertible if and only if $\det(T)\neq0$.

For $0\le k\le n$, the **$k$-th elementary symmetric polynomial** in $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ is

$$e_k(x_1,\ldots,x_n):=\sum_{1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n}x_{i_1}\cdots x_{i_k}.$$

The empty product gives $e_0=1$. We put $e_k=0$ for $k>n$. Each $e_k$ is symmetric because a permutation of the variables merely permutes the $k$-element index sets in the sum.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring in which $n!\,1_R$ is a unit. Then substitution $P_k\mapsto p_k$ is an $R$-algebra isomorphism

$$R[P_1,\ldots,P_n]\longrightarrow R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]^{\operatorname{Sym}_n}.$$

If $R$ is a field, the unit hypothesis is equivalent to $\operatorname{char}R=0$ or $\operatorname{char}R>n$.

Let $R,S$ be commutative rings, let $\varphi:R\to S$ be a ring homomorphism,
and let $(s_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $S$. There is a unique ring homomorphism

$$\Phi:R[x_i:i\in I]\longrightarrow S$$

whose restriction to $R$ is $\varphi$ and which satisfies $\Phi(x_i)=s_i$ for
every $i\in I$.

derivations.claim: [construct] Fix $T_1,\dots,T_n\in W$. For fixed $(v_1,\dots,v_n)\in V^n$ the assignment $T_i\mapsto T_iv_i$ is linear in each variable, so $(T_1,\dots,T_n)\mapsto T_1v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes T_nv_n$ is multilinear in the $T_i$ and its values in $E$ are linear in $(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ separately in each $v_i$; hence there is a unique linear map $\Phi(T_1,\dots,T_n)\in\operatorname{End}(E)$ with the displayed value on every elementary tensor by [F3], and $\Phi$ is multilinear in the $T_i$ because both sides of every identity are checked on the spanning elementary tensors by [F3]. By the representing property of the tensor product [F3] there is a unique linear $\Psi:W^{\otimes n}\to\operatorname{End}(E)$ with $\Psi(T_1\otimes\cdots\otimes T_n)=\Phi(T_1,\dots,T_n)$, which is the map of the Statement; in particular $\Psi$ is linear and is given on elementary tensors as displayed. For $n=0$ one has $W^{\otimes0}=\mathbb C$ and $\Psi(1)=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C}$ by the same universal property.

Let $p:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\sigma\in\operatorname{End}(W^{\otimes n})$, a well-defined operator because $n!\ne0$ in $\mathbb C$; then $p^2=p$, since each group element occurs $n!$ times in the product sum, and $p$ commutes with the action, since left multiplication permutes the summands. Its image is exactly the invariant subspace $(W^{\otimes n})^{S_n}$: $pX$ is invariant for every $X$, and $pX=X$ whenever $X$ is invariant. Thus the invariant tensors are the image of the symmetrization operator. Pure tensors span $W^{\otimes n}$, so their symmetrizations span the image of $p$. For $T_1,\dots,T_n\in W$, inclusion-exclusion gives $$\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}T_{\sigma(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{\sigma(n)} =\sum_{J\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}}(-1)^{n-|J|}\Bigl(\sum_{j\in J}T_j\Bigr)^{\otimes n}.$$ Indeed, after expanding the right side, an ordered tensor survives exactly when every index $1,\dots,n$ occurs, which in a tensor with $n$ factors means each occurs once. Hence each symmetrized pure tensor is a linear combination of powers $T^{\otimes n}$, and $(W^{\otimes n})^{S_n}=\operatorname{span}\{T^{\otimes n}:T\in W\}$. For $n=0$ this equality is immediate in $W^{\otimes0}=\mathbb C$.

The two spans of the Statement are equal. One inclusion is clear, since $\operatorname{GL}(V)\subseteq W$. For the reverse let $T\in W$ and consider the $W^{\otimes n}$-valued polynomial $t\mapsto(T+t\,\mathbf 1_V)^{\otimes n}$; expanding the tensor power of a sum gives $(T+t\,\mathbf 1_V)^{\otimes n}=\sum_{k=0}^nt^kc_k$ with $c_0=T^{\otimes n}$, so it is a polynomial of degree at most $n$ in $t$. The function $t\mapsto\det(t\,\mathbf 1_V+T)$ is a monic polynomial of degree $d=\dim_{\mathbb C}V$ by [F5], hence nonzero with at most $d$ roots by [F5], so by [F6] there exist $n+1$ distinct scalars $t_1,\dots,t_{n+1}$ with $T+t_i\mathbf 1_V$ invertible for all $i$ by [F5] (if $d=0$ then $W=\{0\}$ and $T=0$ is invertible, so any distinct scalars work). For the Lagrange polynomials $L_i(t):=\prod_{j\ne i}(t-t_j)/(t_i-t_j)$ one has $t^k=\sum_i t_i^kL_i(t)$ for every $t$ and every $0\le k\le n$, because it holds at the $n+1$ distinct points and both sides have degree at most $n$; multiplying by $c_k$ and summing gives $T^{\otimes n}=c_0=\sum_iL_i(0)\,(T+t_i\mathbf 1_V)^{\otimes n}\in\operatorname{span}\{g^{\otimes n}:g\in\operatorname{GL}(V)\}$. Hence the two spans are equal.

The matrix units of $W$ with respect to a basis $e_1,\dots,e_d$ of $V$ form a basis of $W$: define $E_{ab}\in W$ by $E_{ab}e_c:=\delta_{bc}e_a$; every $S\in W$ satisfies $S=\sum_{a,b}s_{ab}E_{ab}$ with $s_{ab}$ the coefficients in $S(e_b)=\sum_as_{ab}e_a$, because the two sides agree on each basis vector of $V$, and a relation $\sum_{a,b}\lambda_{ab}E_{ab}=0$ evaluated at $e_b$ gives $\sum_a\lambda_{ab}e_a=0$, so all $\lambda_{ab}=0$. Likewise the endomorphisms $f_{ab}$ of $E$ defined by $f_{ab}(e_{c_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{c_n}):=\delta_{b_1c_1}\cdots\delta_{b_nc_n}\,e_{a_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{a_n}$ for words $a,b\in[d]^n$ form a basis of $\operatorname{End}(E)$, indexed by the finite set $[d]^n\times[d]^n$; for $n=0$ this is the single endomorphism $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C}$ of the one-dimensional space $\mathbb C$, and for $d=0$ and $n\ge1$ all these sets of words are empty and both spaces are zero. By [F2] and [F3] the $d^{2n}$ tensors $E_{a_1b_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes E_{a_nb_n}$ form a basis of $W^{\otimes n}$, and $\Psi$ sends such a tensor to $f_{ab}$ by the formula of step 1.1; a linear map that carries a basis bijectively onto a basis is an isomorphism, so $\Psi$ is a linear isomorphism.

$\Psi$ is $S_n$-equivariant for the place action on $W^{\otimes n}$ and conjugation on $\operatorname{End}(E)$: for $\sigma\in S_n$ and $T_1,\dots,T_n\in W$ the place action gives $\sigma\cdot(T_1\otimes\cdots\otimes T_n)=T_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{\sigma^{-1}(n)}$ by [F1], so by step 1.1 both $\Psi(\sigma\cdot(T_1\otimes\cdots\otimes T_n))$ and $\sigma\Psi(T_1\otimes\cdots\otimes T_n)\sigma^{-1}$ map $v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n$ to $T_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{\sigma^{-1}(n)}v_n$; two linear maps agreeing on the spanning elementary tensors agree, so the identity $\Psi(\sigma\cdot X)=\sigma\Psi(X)\sigma^{-1}$ holds for all $X\in W^{\otimes n}$ by linearity.

For $T\in W$ one has $\Psi(T^{\otimes n})\in A_n$. For $n=0$ this is $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C}\in A_0$, since $A_0$ is unital. Assume $n\ge1$ and put $T_i:=\mathbf 1^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes T\otimes\mathbf 1^{\otimes(n-i)}\in\operatorname{End}(E)$ for $1\le i\le n$; these operators commute pairwise and $\Psi(T^{\otimes n})=T_1T_2\cdots T_n$, while $\sum_{i=1}^nT_i^k=\Delta(T^k)$ for every $k\ge1$, all by the tensor formula of step 1.1 and [F1]. By [F7] with $R=\mathbb C$ (where $n!$ is a unit) there is a polynomial $Q$ in $n$ variables over $\mathbb C$ with $e_n(x_1,\dots,x_n)=Q(p_1,\dots,p_n)$ in $\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_n]$, where $p_k=\sum_i x_i^k$. The operators $T_1,\dots,T_n$ commute, so the $\mathbb C$-subalgebra they generate is commutative, and the universal property of the polynomial ring [F8] gives a $\mathbb C$-algebra homomorphism sending $x_i\mapsto T_i$; it sends $e_n(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ to $T_1\cdots T_n$ by [F7] and $p_k$ to $\Delta(T^k)$, so $T_1\cdots T_n=Q(\Delta(T),\dots,\Delta(T^n))\in A_n$, since each $\Delta(T^k)$ lies in the generating algebra $A_n$ and $Q$ has coefficients in $\mathbb C$.

For $T\in W$ put $d_T:=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes T\otimes\mathbf 1^{\otimes(n-i)}\in W^{\otimes n}$ (the empty sum for $n=0$, giving $d_T=0\in\mathbb C$). Then $\Psi(d_T)=\Delta(T)$ by step 1.1, and $d_T$ is invariant under the place action: a permutation sends the $i$-th summand, which has $T$ in position $i$, to the same kind of summand with $T$ in position $\sigma(i)$ by [F1], and $\sigma$ permutes the index set, so $\sigma\cdot d_T=d_T$. By the equivariance of step 2.2, $\Delta(T)=\Psi(d_T)$ is fixed by conjugation by every $\sigma\in S_n$, that is $\Delta(T)\in\operatorname{End}_{S_n}(E)$; since $\operatorname{End}_{S_n}(E)$ is closed under addition and composition and $A_n$ is generated by the $\Delta(T)$, this gives $A_n\subseteq\operatorname{End}_{S_n}(E)$.

Combining steps: $\Psi$ induces a bijection from $(W^{\otimes n})^{S_n}$ onto $\operatorname{End}_{S_n}(E)$ by step 2.2 and step 2.1, the invariant subspace is $\operatorname{span}\{T^{\otimes n}\}=\operatorname{span}\{g^{\otimes n}\}$ by steps 1.2 and 1.3, and $\Psi(\operatorname{span}\{T^{\otimes n}\})\subseteq A_n\subseteq\operatorname{End}_{S_n}(E)$ by steps 3.1 and 2.3, so all four subspaces of the Statement coincide. For $n=0$: $W^{\otimes0}=E=\mathbb C$, $\Psi$ is the identity, $S_0$ is trivial, $T^{\otimes0}=1$ for every $T$, $\Delta(T)=0$ and $A_0=\mathbb C\,\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C}$, and the displayed chain reads $\mathbb C=\mathbb C=\mathbb C=\mathbb C$. For $V=0$ and $n\ge1$: $W=0$, $E=0$, both sides of the identity are the zero space, and $A_n=0$. This proves both claims.

boundaries.evidence: Step 4.1: for $n=0$, $W^{\otimes0}=E=\mathbb C$, $\Psi$ is the identity, $S_0$ is trivial, $T^{\otimes0}=1$ for every $T$, $\Delta(T)=0$ and $A_0=\mathbb C\,\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C}$, so the displayed chain reads $\mathbb C=\mathbb C=\mathbb C=\mathbb C$.
Step 4.1: for $V=0$ and $n\ge1$, $W=0$, $E=0$, both sides of the identity are the zero space, and $A_n=0$.

Step 1.2: for $n=1$ the symmetrization operator $p=\frac1{1!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_1}\sigma$ is the identity, so the invariant subspace is all of $W$; the chain of step 4.1 then reads $W=W=A_1=\operatorname{End}_{S_1}(E)$.

Step 1.3: the span equality is proved by interpolating $T^{\otimes n}$ through the invertible operators $T+t_i\mathbf 1_V$; the argument covers $d=0$ explicitly and never requires $T$ to be invertible or $V$ to be nonzero.

Step 4.1: the two endpoint cases $n=0$ and $V=0$ are evaluated explicitly, and the inclusion chain $\Psi(\operatorname{span}\{T^{\otimes n}\})\subseteq A_n\subseteq\operatorname{End}_{S_n}(E)$ is closed at both ends to give the equality of all four spaces.
Steps 1.1, 2.1 and 4.1 fix a basis of $V$ and use the finite group $S_n$; the matrix units, $\Psi$ and $p$ are explicit, and no selection principle is invoked.

boundaries.reason: The claims are equalities of subspaces and of algebras, not implications.
No converse is asserted; the 'equivalently' clause rewrites the same equality as a spanning statement.

risk_review.notes: Matrix units identify W⊗n with End(V⊗n). Inclusion-exclusion expresses symmetrized pure tensors through pure powers, interpolation through invertible T+tI gives the GL span, and e_n=x1···xn plus Newton identities places T1···Tn in the algebra generated by Δ(T). The current F7 omits the refuted n! factor; n=0 and V=0 are handled.

citations.quote:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space and let $n\ge0$. Write
$\operatorname{End}(V)$ for the $\mathbb C$-vector space of all linear maps
$V\to V$, and $\operatorname{GL}(V)\subseteq\operatorname{End}(V)$ for the
invertible ones
([[def-finite-dimensional-representation-of-a-group-over-a-field]]).
All tensor products below are over $\mathbb C$.

**The tensor power.** For $n\ge1$ fix the parenthesization
$$E_n\;:=\;V^{\otimes n}\;:=\;\underbrace{V\otimes_{\mathbb C}\cdots\otimes_{\mathbb C}V}_{n\text{ factors}},\qquad V^{\otimes0}\;:=\;\mathbb C,$$
and write $v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n$ for the elementary tensor of
$(v_1,\dots,v_n)\in V^n$; for $n=0$ the unique elementary tensor is $1\in\mathbb C$.
By [[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]] the
assignment $(v_1,\dots,v_n)\mapsto v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n$ is
$\mathbb C$-multilinear and every element of $E_n$ is a finite
$\mathbb C$-linear combination of elementary tensors; for $n=0$ this means
$c=c\cdot1$ for $c\in\mathbb C$. If $e_1,\dots,e_d$ is a $\mathbb C$-basis of
$V$, then by iterating [[thm-tensor-product-basis-from-bases]] the $d^n$ tensors
$e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_n}$ form a $\mathbb C$-basis of $E_n$, so
$E_n$ is finite-dimensional.

**Place permutations: the left $S_n$-action.** Let $S_n$ be the symmetric
group of the set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]). For
$\sigma\in S_n$ define, on elementary tensors,
$$\sigma\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\;:=\;v_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\sigma^{-1}(n)}.$$
The right-hand side depends $\mathbb C$-multilinearly on
$(v_1,\dots,v_n)$, so by the universal property in
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]] there is a
unique $\mathbb C$-linear map $E_n\to E_n$ with this value on every elementary
tensor. Uniqueness is what makes the rule well defined on all of $E_n$, since
the elementary tensors span. The identity permutation acts trivially, and for
$\sigma,\tau\in S_n$ and every elementary tensor,
$$(\sigma\tau)\cdot\bigl(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n\bigr)=v_{(\sigma\tau)^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{(\sigma\tau)^{-1}(n)}=v_{\tau^{-1}(\sigma^{-1}(1))}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\tau^{-1}(\sigma^{-1}(n))},$$
while $\tau\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_{\tau^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\tau^{-1}(n)}$
and hence
$$\sigma\cdot\bigl(\tau\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\bigr)=v_{\tau^{-1}(\sigma^{-1}(1))}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\tau^{-1}(\sigma^{-1}(n))}.$$
The two agree, so the assignments constitute a left action of the group $S_n$
on $E_n$; equivalently $E_n$ is a left module over $S_n$
([[def-finite-dimensional-representation-of-a-group-over-a-field]]).
For $n=0$ the group $S_0$ is trivial and acts on $E_0=\mathbb C$ by the
identity.

**Diagonal linear action.** For $g\in\operatorname{GL}(V)$ define, on
elementary tensors,
$$g^{\otimes n}\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\;:=\;gv_1\otimes\cdots\otimes gv_n,$$
again first on elementary tensors by multilinearity and then uniquely on
$E_n$. Since $g$ and $h$ are linear, the two assignments compose in the
expected way: on elementary tensors,
$$(gh)^{\otimes n}\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=g(hv_1)\otimes\cdots\otimes g(hv_n)=g^{\otimes n}\cdot\bigl(h^{\otimes n}\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\bigr),$$
and $(\mathrm{id}_V)^{\otimes n}$ is the identity. In particular
$(g^{-1})^{\otimes n}$ is the inverse of $g^{\otimes n}$. For $n=0$ every
diagonal operator is the identity on $\mathbb C$.
Thus $g\mapsto g^{\otimes n}$ is a group homomorphism
$\operatorname{GL}(V)\to\operatorname{GL}(E_n)$, that is, a finite-dimensional
representation of the group $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ on $E_n$.

**The two actions commute.** For $\sigma\in S_n$, $g\in\operatorname{GL}(V)$
and an elementary tensor,
$$\sigma\cdot\bigl(g^{\otimes n}\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\bigr)=gv_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes gv_{\sigma^{-1}(n)}=g^{\otimes n}\cdot\bigl(\sigma\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\bigr),$$
so the two linear maps $\sigma\cdot(-)$ and $g^{\otimes n}\cdot(-)$ commute;
equivalently, every $g^{\otimes n}$ is an $S_n$-equivariant endomorphism of
$E_n$ ([[def-intertwiner-equivalent-and-faithful-representations]]).

**The diagonal infinitesimal operator.** For $T\in\operatorname{End}(V)$ put
$$\Delta(T)\;:=\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf 1^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes T\otimes\mathbf 1^{\otimes(n-i)}\ \in\ \operatorname{End}(E_n),$$
where $\mathbf 1=\mathrm{id}_V$ and the sum is $0$ for $n=0$. Each summand
lies in $\operatorname{End}(E_n)$, and $\Delta:\operatorname{End}(V)\to
\operatorname{End}(E_n)$ is $\mathbb C$-linear. It is the first coefficient of
the diagonal action along the line $t\mapsto\mathbf 1+tT$. In this polynomial
calculation, $(\mathbf 1+tT)^{\otimes n}$ is the tensor power of the
endomorphism $\mathbf 1+tT$; it agrees with the $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ action
whenever that endomorphism is invertible. For every $t\in\mathbb C$ one
computes, on elementary tensors,
$$(\mathbf 1+tT)^{\otimes n}\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}t^k\sum_{1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n}w_{i_1,\dots,i_k},\qquad (w_{i_1,\dots,i_k})_j=\begin{cases}Tv_j,&j\in\{i_1,\dots,i_k\},\\ v_j,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
the coefficient of $t$ being $\Delta(T)\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)$
(zero when $n=0$); both sides
are polynomials in $t$ with values in the finite-dimensional space $E_n$
described on a spanning set. Finally let
$$A_n\;:=\;\text{the unital }\mathbb C\text{-subalgebra of }\operatorname{End}(E_n)\text{ generated by }\{\Delta(T):T\in\operatorname{End}(V)\};$$
this is the image of the diagonal action of the universal enveloping algebra
$U(\mathfrak{gl}(V))$ on $E_n$, defined here as that generated algebra, with
no Lie-theoretic input.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space, let $n\ge0$, and let
$E:=V^{\otimes n}$ carry the left place action of $S_n$
([[def-commuting-symmetric-and-linear-actions-on-tensor-power]]). Write
$W:=\operatorname{End}(V)$ and let
$\operatorname{End}_{S_n}(E):=\{F\in\operatorname{End}(E):\sigma F=F\sigma
\text{ for all }\sigma\in S_n\}$ be the centralizer of the action. Then:

1. **(Canonical identification.)** The linear map
   $\Psi:W^{\otimes n}\to\operatorname{End}(E)$ with
   $\Psi(T_1\otimes\cdots\otimes T_n)(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)
   =T_1v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes T_nv_n$ on elementary tensors is a linear
   isomorphism, and it is equivariant for the place action of $S_n$ on
   $W^{\otimes n}$ and conjugation $F\mapsto\sigma F\sigma^{-1}$ on
   $\operatorname{End}(E)$. Hence $\Psi$ restricts to an isomorphism from the
   invariant tensors, that is from the image of the symmetrization operator
   $\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\sigma$ on $W^{\otimes n}$ (the $n$-th
   symmetric tensor power of $W$), onto $\operatorname{End}_{S_n}(E)$.
2. **(Spans.)** The subspaces $\operatorname{span}\{T^{\otimes n}:T\in W\}$
   and $\operatorname{span}\{g^{\otimes n}:g\in\operatorname{GL}(V)\}$ of
   $W^{\otimes n}$ are both equal to the invariant tensors; equivalently, with
   $\Delta(T)=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes T\otimes\mathbf 1^{\otimes(n-i)}$
   and $A_n$ the unital $\mathbb C$-subalgebra of $\operatorname{End}(E)$
   generated by all $\Delta(T)$ (the image of the diagonal action of
   $U(\mathfrak{gl}(V))$ as defined there,
   [[def-commuting-symmetric-and-linear-actions-on-tensor-power]]),
   $$\textstyle\operatorname{End}_{S_n}(E)=\Psi(\operatorname{span}\{T^{\otimes n}:T\in W\})=\Psi(\operatorname{span}\{g^{\otimes n}:g\in\operatorname{GL}(V)\})=A_n.$$

All statements include $n=0$, where $W^{\otimes0}=\mathbb C$ and $E=\mathbb C$,
and the case $V=0$.

Let $G$ be a finite group, let $k$ be a field with
$\operatorname{char} k \nmid |G|$, let $\rho:G \to \operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a
finite-dimensional representation of $G$ over $k$, and let $W \le V$ be a
subrepresentation. Then there is a subrepresentation $U \le V$ such that

$$V=W\oplus U.$$

For every $n\ge0$, the modules $\{S^\lambda:\lambda\vdash n\}$ form a
complete irredundant list, up to isomorphism, of finite-dimensional irreducible
complex $S_n$-representations.

Let $V$ and $W$ be irreducible representations of a group $G$ over a field $k$.
Then every nonzero intertwiner $f:V \to W$ is an isomorphism. Consequently
$\operatorname{End}_G(V)$ is a division ring.

Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field, let $G$ be a group, and let $V$ be an
irreducible representation of $G$ over $k$. Then every $T \in \operatorname{End}_G(V)$
is of the form $T=\lambda \operatorname{id}_V$ for some $\lambda \in k$.

Let $V$ be a completely reducible representation of a group $G$ over a field
$k$. If $S_1,\ldots,S_r$ represent the distinct equivalence classes of
irreducible subrepresentations occurring in $V$, then

$$V=V_{(S_1)}\oplus\cdots\oplus V_{(S_r)}.$$

Moreover each summand $V_{(S_i)}$ depends only on the equivalence class of
$S_i$, so this isotypic decomposition is independent of the chosen
decomposition of $V$ into irreducible summands.

Let $N$ be a finite group, let $S$ be an irreducible complex $N$-module with character $\theta$, and let $U$ be a finite-dimensional $\theta$-isotypical $N$-module, allowing $U=0$. Put $M=\operatorname{Hom}_N(S,U)$ and give $M$ the trivial $N$-action. Evaluation is an $N$-isomorphism
$$ E_U:S\otimes_{\mathbb C}M\longrightarrow U,\qquad s\otimes f\longmapsto f(s). $$
Every $N$-submodule $U_0\subseteq U$ is $E_U(S\otimes M_0)$ for a unique subspace $M_0\subseteq M$, namely $M_0=\operatorname{Hom}_N(S,U_0)$ viewed inside $M$ by inclusion. If $U^\prime$ is another such module and $M^\prime=\operatorname{Hom}_N(S,U')$, then every $N$-map $U\to U'$ is uniquely $E_{U'}(1_S\otimes a)E_U^{-1}$ for a linear map $a:M\to M^\prime$. These identifications preserve composition.

Let $G$ be a finite group and let $k$ be an algebraically closed field with
$\operatorname{char} k \nmid |G|$. Then there are positive integers
$n_1,\ldots,n_r$ such that

$$ k[G]\cong\prod_{i=1}^r M_{n_i}(k) $$

as $k$-algebras.

Let $r\ge1$, let every $n_i\ge1$, let every $D_i$ be a division ring, and put $R=\prod_{i=1}^rM_{n_i}(D_i)$. Then every simple left $R$-module is supported on exactly one factor and is isomorphic to that factor's column module $D_i^{n_i}$. These column modules give all simple left $R$-module isomorphism classes, with one class for each factor. See [[thm-wedderburn-artin-theorem]].

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $G$ be a group, and let $M$ be a left
$R$-module. Then:

1. every $R$-linear action of $G$ on $M$ extends uniquely to a left
   $R[G]$-module structure on $M$ satisfying
   $$(r[e]) \cdot m=rm\qquad(r \in R,\ m \in M);$$
2. every left $R[G]$-module structure on $M$ satisfying
   $$(r[e]) \cdot m=rm\qquad(r \in R,\ m \in M)$$
   restricts to an $R$-linear action of $G$ on $M$;
3. these two constructions are inverse to each other.

Moreover, if $M$ and $N$ carry the corresponding structures, then an
$R$-linear map $f:M \to N$ is $G$-equivariant if and only if it is an
$R[G]$-module homomorphism.

Let $k$ be a field, let $G$ be a group, and let $V$ be a finite-dimensional
representation of $G$ over $k$. Under the correspondence of
[[thm-group-actions-and-group-ring-modules-correspond]]:

1. the subrepresentations of $V$ are exactly the $k[G]$-submodules of $V$;
2. $V$ is irreducible if and only if it is simple as a $k[G]$-module.

derivations.claim: [construct] Recall that $A$ is a unital subalgebra of $\operatorname{End}(E)$, because it is the image of a unital algebra homomorphism, and that $B$ is a unital subalgebra, because $g^{\otimes n}h^{\otimes n}=(gh)^{\otimes n}$ for $g,h\in\operatorname{GL}(V)$; both contain $\mathbf 1_E$ (for $B$ take $g=1_V$, and for $n=0$ note $g^{\otimes0}=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C}$ for every $g$ and $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ is nonempty).

By [F3] the $\mathbb C[S_n]$-module $E$ is completely reducible, so by [F4] and the uniqueness of the isotypic decomposition in [F6] there are subspaces $E_\lambda$ for $\lambda$ in the finite set $\Lambda:=\{\lambda\vdash n:\operatorname{Hom}_{S_n}(S^\lambda,E)\ne0\}$ with $E=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda}E_\lambda$, each $E_\lambda$ is $\lambda$-isotypical, and the evaluation maps of [F6] give $S_n$-isomorphisms $E_\lambda\cong S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda$ with $M_\lambda:=\operatorname{Hom}_{S_n}(S^\lambda,E)$ carrying the trivial action; consequently the action of $\sigma\in S_n$ on $E_\lambda$ corresponds to $\rho_\lambda(\sigma)\otimes\mathbf 1_{M_\lambda}$, where $\rho_\lambda$ is the action on the irreducible $S^\lambda$.

The simple left $\mathbb C[S_n]$-modules are, by [F7], the column modules of the factors of a decomposition $\mathbb C[S_n]\cong\prod_{i=1}^rM_{n_i}(\mathbb C)$, one class per factor and each supported on one factor; by [F8] the irreducible complex representations of the group $S_n$ are exactly the simple left $\mathbb C[S_n]$-modules, so by [F4] the isomorphism classes of simple left $\mathbb C[S_n]$-modules are exactly the classes $[S^\lambda]$, $\lambda\vdash n$. Hence the factors are indexed by the partitions of $n$, with $n_i=\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\lambda$ for the factor attached to $\lambda$, and $\dim_{\mathbb C}\mathbb C[S_n]=\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}(\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\lambda)^2$.

An endomorphism $T\in\operatorname{End}(S\otimes M)$ of a tensor product, $S,M$ finite-dimensional over $\mathbb C$ with $M\ne0$, commuting with $\mathbf 1_S\otimes b$ for all $b\in\operatorname{End}(M)$ is of the form $T=x\otimes\mathbf 1_M$ for a unique $x\in\operatorname{End}(S)$: choose bases $s_1,\ldots,s_p$ of $S$ and $m_1,\ldots,m_q$ of $M$ (both finite, with $q\ge1$), write $T(s\otimes m_1)=\sum_{j=1}^qx_j(s)\otimes m_j$ with well-defined linear maps $x_j:S\to S$; for each $j$ let $b_j\in\operatorname{End}(M)$ be given on the basis by $b_j(m_1)=m_j$ and $b_j(m_i)=0$ for $i\ge2$; then $T(s\otimes m_j)=T((\mathbf 1\otimes b_j)(s\otimes m_1))=(\mathbf 1\otimes b_j)T(s\otimes m_1)=x_1(s)\otimes m_j$, so $T=x_1\otimes\mathbf 1_M$ on all basis vectors, and conversely every $x\otimes\mathbf 1_M$ commutes with the operators $\mathbf 1\otimes b$.

The first displayed identity of claim 1 holds: a map $F\in\operatorname{End}(E)$ commutes with every $a\in A$ exactly when it commutes with $\sigma$ for every $\sigma\in S_n$, because $A$ is the linear span of the place operators $\sigma$; hence the centralizer of $A$ is $\operatorname{End}_{S_n}(E)$, which equals $B$ by [F2]. The same fact of [F2] identifies $B$ with the image of the diagonal action of $U(\mathfrak{gl}(V))$, so claim 2 holds; in particular $B$ is a subalgebra, in agreement with step 1.1.

The canonical algebra homomorphism $\Phi:\mathbb C[S_n]\to\prod_{\lambda\vdash n}\operatorname{End}(S^\lambda)$, $\Phi(x)=(\rho_\lambda(x))_{\lambda}$, is an isomorphism. It is injective: if $x$ acts as $0$ on every $S^\lambda$, then under the product decomposition of step 1.3 the element $x$ has a component in each factor which annihilates that factor's own column module, and so is $0$, so $x=0$; here [F8] identifies the column module of the factor attached to $\lambda$ with the simple module $S^\lambda$, on which $x$ acts as $\rho_\lambda(x)$ by definition of $\Phi$. It is then bijective because, by step 1.3 and $\dim_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{End}(S^\lambda)=(\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\lambda)^2$, source and target have the same finite dimension $\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}(\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\lambda)^2$.

The algebra $\operatorname{End}_{S_n}(E)$ is $\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\operatorname{End}(M_\lambda)$: an $S_n$-endomorphism of $E$ maps each isotypic component $E_\lambda$ into itself, since the image of a copy of $S^\lambda$ is $0$ or a copy of $S^\lambda$ by [F5] and [F4]; on $E_\lambda$ it is, by [F6] and step 1.2, exactly the operator induced by a unique $a_\lambda\in\operatorname{End}(M_\lambda)$ on the second tensor factor; maps between distinct components $E_\lambda\to E_\mu$ are zero by [F5] and [F4] because $S^\lambda$ and $S^\mu$ are non-isomorphic for $\lambda\ne\mu$; and the identifications preserve composition, so this is an algebra isomorphism under which $a_\lambda$ corresponds to the operator $\mathbf 1_{S^\lambda}\otimes a_\lambda$ on $E_\lambda$. In particular, by step 2.1, $B$ is exactly the set of operators $\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda}(\mathbf 1_{S^\lambda}\otimes b_\lambda)$ with $b_\lambda\in\operatorname{End}(M_\lambda)$.

Under the isomorphism $\Phi$ of step 2.2 and the isomorphisms $E_\lambda\cong S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda$ of step 1.2, the action of $x\in\mathbb C[S_n]$ on $E=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda}E_\lambda$ is $\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda}(\rho_\lambda(x)\otimes\mathbf 1_{M_\lambda})$, the factors with $\lambda\notin\Lambda$ acting on no summand; hence the image $A$ of this action map is exactly $$A=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\bigl(\operatorname{End}(S^\lambda)\otimes\mathbf 1_{M_\lambda}\bigr)\subseteq\operatorname{End}(E),$$ the direct sum of the indicated block subalgebras indexed by $\Lambda$: indeed the projection $\prod_{\lambda\vdash n}\operatorname{End}(S^\lambda)\to\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\operatorname{End}(S^\lambda)$ is surjective and $\Phi$ is an isomorphism.

Commutation with block-supported elements of B forces every off-diagonal block F_{mu,lambda} to vanish. Each diagonal block F_{lambda,lambda} commutes with 1_{S^lambda} tensor b for every b in End(M_lambda), because B contains every such operator supported on that block.

By steps 4.1 and 1.4 the centralizer of $B$ consists exactly of the elements $\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda}(x_\lambda\otimes\mathbf 1_{M_\lambda})$ with $x_\lambda\in\operatorname{End}(S^\lambda)$, which is exactly $A$ by step 3.2; this proves the second identity of claim 1, and claim 2 was proved in step 2.1.

Boundary and choice audit. For $n=0$ one has $E=V^{\otimes0}=\mathbb C$, $A=B=\mathbb C\,\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C}=\operatorname{End}(E)$ and both centralizers equal the whole of $\operatorname{End}(E)$, in agreement with claims 1 and 2; the case is covered by the argument with $\Lambda=\{(\varnothing)\}$ when $\operatorname{Hom}_{S_0}(S^\varnothing,\mathbb C)=\mathbb C$. For $V=0$ and $n\ge1$ one has $E=0$, so $\operatorname{End}(E)=0=A=B$ by [F2] and all assertions hold; here $\Lambda=\varnothing$, the products over $\Lambda$ are the zero algebra, and steps 4.1 and 1.4 are vacuous. For $V\ne0$ and $n\ge1$, every $\lambda\in\Lambda$ has $M_\lambda\ne0$ by definition, so step 1.4 applies with $M=M_\lambda$. All bases and decompositions used are attached to finite-dimensional spaces and to the finitely many partitions of $n$; the decomposition of $E$ and the factors of $\mathbb C[S_n]$ are canonical, and no choice principle is invoked.
